title: CQRS Pattern: CommandBus, QueryBus, EventBus, and Sagas

progressiveExplaining.eli5: In a busy restaurant, ordering food (making changes to the kitchen) uses a completely separate order counter than asking 'what are the daily specials?' (reading data). CQRS splits your application into two lanes: **Commands** (do something / mutate) and **Queries** (read something / fast view), keeping massive systems clean and organized.
progressiveExplaining.junior: The CQRS package (`@nestjs/cqrs`) separates read and write operations. **Commands** represent state-changing actions executed via `CommandBus.execute(new CreateUserCommand(data))`. **Queries** represent read-only operations executed via `QueryBus.execute(new GetUserQuery(id))`. **Events** announce past occurrences via `EventBus.publish(new UserCreatedEvent(id))`. **Sagas** listen to events and trigger subsequent commands asynchronously.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, CQRS enforces strict Command-Query Separation (CQS) at the domain level. Commands have dedicated single-responsibility `ICommandHandler` implementations, ensuring write models contain domain validation and business invariants without query-joining clutter. Queries use dedicated `IQueryHandler` implementations optimized for direct database views or read replicas. Sagas are RxJS stream processors (`@Saga()`) coordinating long-running, multi-service distributed transactions.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: The `CqrsModule` maintains internal handler registries (`Map<string, ICommandHandler>`). When `commandBus.execute(command)` is called, it resolves the command constructor name, locates the registered handler from the IoC container, executes `handler.execute(command)`, and returns the promise. Sagas subscribe to the global `EventBus` stream (`events$.pipe(ofType(...), map(...))`), automatically dispatching mapped output commands into the `CommandBus`.

codeComparison.title: Monolithic Service with Mixed Read/Write vs Clean CQRS Handlers
codeComparison.summary: Monolithic services become bloated with hundreds of mixed methods; CQRS breaks features into isolated command and query handlers.

interviewGotchas.question: What is a 'Saga' in the NestJS CQRS architecture and how does it differ from an Event Handler?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers test your knowledge of event-driven distributed transactions.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: An **Event Handler** (`@EventsHandler`) is a terminal listener that performs side effects (e.g. sending an email or writing a log) when an event occurs. A **Saga** (`@Saga()`) is an RxJS stream operator that listens to events and **translates them into NEW Commands** to be dispatched to the `CommandBus`. Sagas orchestrate multi-step, asynchronous business workflows (e.g. `OrderCreatedEvent` -> maps to -> `ExecutePaymentCommand`).
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: A Saga must return an `Observable<ICommand>`. If a saga returns `void`, it will not dispatch commands.

interviewGotchas.question: Can multiple Command Handlers handle the same Command in NestJS?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Checks precision regarding Command vs Event semantics in CQRS.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: **No.** In CQRS, a **Command has exactly ONE handler** (1:1 relationship) because a command represents an explicit intent to mutate state. An **Event can have ZERO or MANY handlers** (1:N broadcast relationship) because an event represents a past fact that multiple components may react to.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Registering two handlers for the same `ICommand` will throw a runtime error in NestJS.
